content.text: While I intend on starting with Mary Boas' math methods textbook for my reading list, I don't have it yet so I read the first 2 chapters of "Elementary Differential Equations and Boundary Value Problems" by DiPrima and Boyce today instead. I've taken a differential equations course before so none of this was new to me but it is a good refresher. I'll also say that I took the derivations more seriously than I did when I took the course and I was happy to find that I could derive all of the theorems and methods so far with minimal guidance from the book. It was especially neat to derive the integrating factor method for solving linear first order ODEs since I remember using this method in college and thinking it felt a bit like magic. I think that's primarily because, even though we derived it then, the steps we took to derive it seem completely arbitrary and more like lucky guesses. This book had a neat way of solving an example problem, pointing out interesting properties about the solution, then testing if those properties generalize to all 1st order linear ODEs, that way the motivation for each step of the derivation is clear.

content.caption: Phone image of the moon through my celestron

content.text: Tonight I also used my new (to me) 'Celestron Power Seeker 127EQ' for the first time to see the full moon. I'm still astonished to see it so closely. The prominence of Tycho crater conjures so many thoughts. I wonder where the asteroid that caused Tycho crater originated, how far/long had it been traveling before it hit the moon? Did any debris from the impact land on earth? Imagine what it would have looked like from earth to see that. Google says the impact was a hair over 100 million years ago, so while there were no humans, there was a creature that looked up in the night sky and saw fire and debris shooting from the moon. I wonder what it would have thought. Something about the celestial bodies makes me appreciate being a living human being like nothing else. Under the weight of the heavenly bodies my worldly problems seem so frivolous. That the universe is so awe inspiring, and that I am alive to see it. I feel like the luckiest thing in the universe.
